Coeur d'Alene

The Coeur d’Alene Tribe identifies itself as Schitsu’umsh, “Those who were found here.” This guide follows the Tribe’s own public accounts of homeland, governance and language alongside historical agreements, a Supreme Court decision, a tribal-authored history and environmental records. The sources describe different periods and kinds of evidence; none of the regional or legal summaries is a complete map of community history.

Still unfinished

Fifteen substantive works were inspected, including multiple Coeur d’Alene Tribe publications, two agreement texts, a Supreme Court opinion, a tribal-authored position preserved in a federal EIS, and EPA cleanup records. The collection now supports a useful, cited introduction to identity, language, land, governance and environmental history, but the evidence is uneven across periods and subjects. Source quantity alone does not make the research complete or community-reviewed.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The Tribe’s history, history-page acreage descriptions and older legal records need fuller comparison with community-authored histories and archival records.
  • Archaeology, family histories, foodways, arts, and community perspectives beyond the selected public materials remain underrepresented.
  • The 1995 EIS contains sensitive cultural-resource detail and dated governmental framing; the public summary omits locations and should not be treated as a full account.
  • Current constitutional and governmental details should be verified against current Tribe publications before being stated as current.
  • Environmental cleanup figures and schedules change; this guide preserves a 2024 bulletin as a dated snapshot and EPA’s live status as reviewed October 23, 2026.

Seltice, Chief of the Coeur D’Alênes, 1891
Olin Levi Warner, 1891. Smithsonian American Art Museum, A Gift of Alison Warner Waterman in memory of her mother, Frances D. Warner, 1985.76.3. Public domain.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Museum photograph of Olin Levi Warner’s 1891 bronze portrait relief of the specifically identified Coeur d’Alene leader Seltice. This is an outside sculptor’s historical portrait, not Coeur d’Alene-made art, a photograph of the living sitter, or a present government representation. The museum’s curators place Warner’s portraits in the context of racial classification and an erroneous expectation that Native peoples would disappear, and note that the sitters’ perspectives are poorly documented. That context is retained; no essential cultural or physical trait is inferred from the portrait. No traditional design meanings or community endorsement are claimed. Complete delivered 2600x2600 source frame preserved. Web JPEG resized proportionally to 1800x1800 and recompressed at quality 88; no pixel crop, generated material, retouching or added detail. Cards and opened-page backgrounds may use disclosed CSS crops/overlays. Visual review does not add substantive research counts or community endorsement. The original download endpoint returned a short Request Rejected HTML page instead of an image. No retry or challenge bypass was attempted. The separate public display URL returned directly by the same item API worked and supplied the inspected complete display frame. No claim that the original full-resolution file was inspected.

01

Names, community and living government

The Tribe’s public “Our Tribe” page uses Schitsu’umsh and explains the English name “Coeur d’Alene” as a French label applied by outsiders. The Tribe describes a continuing people with its own government and language. These are the community’s own public descriptions. A 1947 constitution scan records an earlier formal government structure; its text is a historical document, and current government or membership rules should be checked against current tribal publications rather than inferred from this edition.

Read the sources [1] Coeur d’Alene Tribe [9] Coeur d’Alene Tribe; Library of Congress digital copy

02

Homeland, waterways and historical change

The Tribe describes a homeland organized around waterways, villages, trade and seasonal relationships. Its ancestral-lands page and 2012 Integrated Resource Management Plan emphasize continuing relationships with land and water while recounting later cessions and the loss of land access. The Tribe’s acreage descriptions vary by document and method; they should be read as attributed community or planning statements, not fixed boundaries. Public historical agreements also record proposed or conditional arrangements. Read together, these records show colonial-era legal changes without implying that a document alone captures consent, lived experience or the full extent of homeland.

Read the sources [3] Coeur d’Alene Tribe [8] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Natural Resources Department [10] Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75 [11] Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75

03

Language, writing and teaching

The Tribe’s language materials distinguish the Coeur d’Alene language from the larger Salish language family and from neighboring languages. A tribal account describes documentation and orthography work by Lawrence G. Nicodemus and Joseph N. Bitar, and the Tribe’s elementary curriculum page describes a four-year STEP grant and a Tribe-created social-studies curriculum. These sources document published approaches and a dated program; they do not measure present language fluency or establish current program availability. The brief language overview is retained as a starting point but is not counted as a substantive work.

Read the sources [5] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Culture Department [6] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Culture Department [7] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Department of Education [4] Coeur d’Alene Tribe

04

Agreements, reservation history and a defined legal holding

The July 1873 agreement proposed a reservation and included terms subject to further federal action; the archive records it as not ratified. The September 1889 agreement described a northern land cession and made its operation conditional on ratification of an earlier agreement. These are primary texts, useful for studying what their signatories and drafters wrote, not self-explanatory accounts of consent. In Idaho v. United States (2001), the Supreme Court held that the United States holds specified submerged lands within the current reservation in trust for the Tribe. That decision concerns submerged-land title within reservation boundaries; it does not decide ownership of the entire lake or every water and land interest in the basin.

Read the sources [10] Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75 [11] Oklahoma State University, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; underlying record cited to NARA RG 75 [12] Supreme Court of the United States

05

Stewardship, mining and environmental history

The Tribe’s resource plan and its public lake-management account describe relationships among land, water, health and cultural resources, as well as the effects of mining and dam operations. A 1995 federal environmental review preserves a tribal position statement and a history attributed to Bingo Sijohn; these are important, specifically attributed tribal perspectives inside a government compilation. The EPA’s Bunker Hill record independently documents mining-related contamination, cleanup actions and continuing risks across the basin. EPA figures and work status change over time, so its live site and its July 2024 bulletin are dated snapshots. The compiled exhibits contain sensitive cultural-resource details; this guide does not reproduce those locations.

Read the sources [8] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Natural Resources Department [13] Bureau of Reclamation, Bonneville Power Administration and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, System Operation Review Final EIS exhibits; includes Tribe-submitted material [14] Coeur d’Alene Tribe [15] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency [16] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 10

06

How to read this collection

Begin with the Tribe’s own identity, land and language pages, then compare its planning documents with the agreements and court opinion. Use the EPA records for environmental cleanup history and the 1995 exhibits for the Tribe’s position as it was submitted in that review. The constitution, agreements and court decision each answer different legal or historical questions. Dates, authorship and selected-page limits matter throughout; none of these works alone represents every family, period or current community perspective.

Reviewed 15 substantive works and three short supporting references on 2026-10-23. The substantive count is separate from adequacy, completion, and community review. Source roles are intentionally distinguished: the Tribe’s own accounts describe community perspective; agreements and the 1947 constitution are historical texts; Idaho v. United States is a narrow legal holding; EPA records describe cleanup administration and status. The 2012 IRMP was inspected only on selected pages 15–16, 66, and 188–190. The 1995 EIS exhibits were inspected on selected PDF pages 143–165. Neither review represents reading every page. No new historical map association was added. Existing map and regional records remain unchanged.

Primary legal decisionSupreme Court of the United StatesSource 12

Idaho v. United States, 533 U.S. 262 ↗

Publication: 2001

Read the opinion in volume 533, pp. 262–280 (bound PDF pp. 265–280 in an 868-page volume). The Court held that the United States holds in trust for the Tribe the specified submerged lands within the reservation, including portions of the lake and river. The holding is limited to title in the disputed submerged lands; it is not a ruling that the Tribe owns the whole lake or every basin interest.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope
